articles.title: Médico preso em Suzano por suspeita de abuso sexual em hospital | G1
articles.standfirst: Prefeitura exigiu o desligamento do profissional, que atuava na unidade havia cerca de seis meses. Mulher de 32 anos procurou atendimento após diagnóstico de pedra nos rins.
articles.summary: O médico preso em Suzano foi desligado após paciente de 32 anos denunciar abuso sexual durante atendimento para pedra nos rins em hospital municipal.
articles.body:
O médico Rubens Sousa de Oliveira, de 63 anos, foi preso em flagrante nesta quarta-feira (14), suspeito de abusar sexualmente de uma paciente de 32 anos durante um atendimento no Hospital e Maternidade de Suzano (HMS). Segundo a mulher, ele tocou a região íntima dela durante uma consulta de retorno após um diagnóstico de pedra nos rins.

O caso foi registrado como importunação sexual na Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher (DDM) de Suzano. O médico passará por audiência de custódia nesta quinta-feira (15). De acordo com a Polícia Civil, o advogado de Rubens não esteve na unidade e informou que o representaria na audiência custódia. O g1 tenta localizar a defesa do médico.

A Prefeitura de Suzano informou que a Controladoria Geral do Município exigiu o desligamento imediato do médico, que é vinculado a uma empresa terceirizada prestadora de serviços (leia mais abaixo) .

Rubens Sousa de Oliveira, de 63 anos, foi preso suspeito de abusar sexualmente de uma paciente em Suzano — Foto: Reprodução/CRM-SP

A paciente contou que procurou atendimento na quarta-feira anterior (7), porque sentia muitas dores, e descobriu que estava com pedra nos rins. Como também havia suspeita de apendicite, ela passou por exames e foi atendida pelo cirurgião.

Segundo a mulher, durante a primeira consulta, o médico passou a mão duas ou três vezes próximo ao seio dela enquanto examinava sua barriga. Ela estava sem sutiã por causa da tomografia e, naquele momento, acreditou que os toques tinham sido acidentais.

Ainda conforme o relato, o médico pediu que ela retornasse ao hospital uma semana depois, às 6h, para que ele solicitasse um ultrassom.

Nesta quarta-feira, uma enfermeira estava na sala no início do atendimento, mas saiu. A paciente disse que o médico pediu que ela se deitasse na maca e examinou sua barriga e a região da pélvis.

De acordo com a mulher, ele pediu que ela se virasse de bruços e fechou completamente a porta. Em seguida, abaixou a calça dela, tocou sua região íntima com movimentos circulares e pediu que ela movimentasse o corpo da mesma forma.

A paciente afirmou que sentiu desconforto e ficou com a região íntima dolorida. Segundo ela, o médico retirou a mão quando a enfermeira voltou à sala e encerrou o atendimento.

Ao sair, a mulher começou a chorar e ligou para a noiva, que a orientou a procurar alguém do hospital. Ela chamou a enfermeira que havia acompanhado parte da consulta, relatou o que aconteceu e perguntou se aquilo fazia parte do atendimento para pedra nos rins.

Segundo a paciente, as enfermeiras disseram que aquela não era uma conduta normal para esse tipo de exame. Elas acionaram a assistência social do hospital e tentaram entrar em contato com a coordenação.

A mulher afirmou que decidiu denunciar o caso, e a Patrulha Maria da Penha, da Guarda Civil Municipal (GCM), foi acionada e conduziu o médico à DDM.

Caso aconteceu no no Hospital e Maternidade de Suzano — Foto: Wanderley Costa/Prefeitura de Suzano

A Prefeitura de Suzano informou que a Controladoria Geral do Município exigiu o desligamento imediato do médico, que é vinculado a uma empresa terceirizada prestadora de serviços. A administração municipal afirmou que acompanha as providências junto à entidade gestora do hospital e à empresa responsável.

Segundo a prefeitura, o profissional atua na unidade há aproximadamente seis meses e realizou menos de 25 plantões nesse período. A administração municipal disse que, até então, não havia registro de denúncia contra ele.

A prefeitura afirmou que fiscaliza os serviços prestados, exige documentação e verifica o histórico profissional dos médicos que atuam na unidade, conforme os critérios administrativos e contratuais.

Ainda segundo a administração municipal, os próprios profissionais do hospital acionaram a Guarda Civil Municipal (GCM). Agentes da Patrulha Maria da Penha foram à unidade, prenderam o suspeito em flagrante e o levaram à Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher (DDM), onde a autoridade policial confirmou a prisão.

A paciente recebeu assistência da equipe hospitalar, com acompanhamento dos serviços social e psicológico, além de apoio durante o encaminhamento à delegacia, de acordo com a prefeitura.

Em nota, a administração municipal repudiou qualquer forma de violência contra a mulher e afirmou que vai colaborar com a investigação, preservando a identidade, a privacidade e os direitos da paciente.

articles.title: Out on bail in murder case, man stabbed and shot dead outside Ulhasnagar railway station near Mumbai
articles.summary: Murder accused on bail, Haresh Gajwani, stabbed and shot dead outside Ulhasnagar railway station; police probe possible motive linked to 2021 case.
articles.body: ULHASNAGAR: An accused in a murder case, Haresh Gajwani (54) alias Gajya, was stabbed and shot dead by unidentified assailants outside Ulhasnagar railway station on Wednesday night.The attackers allegedly first assaulted Gajwani with a chopper before firing two rounds at him, one of which hit him, while the other misfired, Vitthalwadi police said. Gajwani was rushed to Central Hospital by locals and police, where doctors declared him “brought dead”. A senior police officer said that they are checking CCTV footage of the area to track down the culprits.Gajwani had reportedly launched campaigns against the illegal sale of gutka, gambling and online gambling in the locality. He was allegedly receiving threats following his efforts to expose these activities, local residents said.Deputy commissioner of police Sachin Gore said Gajwani had a criminal record and a murder case had been registered against him in 2021, in which he was out on bail. Police suspect that the killing may have stemmed from a dispute linked to this case, but are investigating all possible angles, Gore said.Gajwani, who lived with his wife and daughter in Ambernath, had earlier resided in Ulhasnagar’s Camp 4 area, where he was actively involved in social work.Recently, he had posted on X about the alleged illegal activities in the area and claimed that some police personnel were supporting those involved. He had tagged senior officials from various police departments as well as the chief minister, deputy chief minister and FDA commissioner Tukaram Mundhe. In his posts, he had also expressed fear for his life, warning that the police personnel he had accused should also be held responsible if anything happened to him.His foster sister, Rajni Thakur, told TOI that Gajwani had been working for the welfare of society and had raised his voice against certain people, following which he had allegedly received threats. She demanded a thorough investigation and strict action against those responsible for his murder.Gajwani’s elder son, who suffered from thalassemia, died three years ago after battling the illness for 13 years.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Macaé avança na consolidação da política pública de cuidados paliativos | G1
articles.standfirst: Após realizar 1ª Conferência Municipal sobre o tema, cidade integra atendimentos do HPM à rede de saúde para promover cuidado humanizado no SUS.
articles.summary: Após realizar 1ª Conferência Municipal sobre o tema, cidade integra atendimentos do HPM à rede de saúde para promover cuidado humanizado no SUS.
articles.body:
Debates municipais alinharam a integração da assistência paliativa entre o HPM e a rede de saúde — Foto: Arquivo Secom

Macaé deu mais um passo importante no fortalecimento da saúde pública com a realização da 1ª Conferência Municipal de Cuidados Paliativos. O encontro reuniu especialistas, gestores e equipes multiprofissionais com o objetivo de alinhar as diretrizes da Política Nacional de Cuidados Paliativos e estruturar a integração contínua desses serviços na rede municipal.

As práticas de atendimento especializado para o controle da dor e o amparo emocional, social e espiritual a pacientes com doenças graves e suas famílias já são aplicadas no Hospital Público Municipal (HPM). A conferência deu sequência ao trabalho de estruturação iniciado pela prefeitura, que já conta com uma Comissão Municipal de Cuidados Paliativos e uma cartilha orientadora aprovada para os profissionais de saúde do município.

Equipes do Polo de Oncologia e do HPM abordaram práticas de atenção humanizada para crianças e adultos — Foto: Arquivo Secom

Durante o ciclo de palestras, médicos, fisioterapeutas e psicólogos debateram temas estratégicos como a atuação da reabilitação física na manutenção do conforto do paciente, o suporte a crianças com condições crônicas complexas e a aplicação da Terapia da Dignidade.

Servidores e técnicos do Polo Municipal de Oncologia também participaram ativamente das discussões. A Coordenação Municipal de Cuidados Paliativos destaca que os desdobramentos da conferência visam consolidar a atuação multiprofissional e expandir o modelo humanizado do HPM para outros pontos da rede de saúde. O objetivo é assegurar que os pacientes que necessitam desse acompanhament

articles.title: Kenya’s Ebola cases test preparedness beyond Nairobi
articles.summary: The scare exposed gaps in how far outbreak readiness reaches Kenya’s remote communities.
articles.body:
Nairobi, Kenya – Kenya’s response to an imported Ebola case has demonstrated its ability to mobilise a national response in the capital.

But a suspected case in the northeastern county of Wajir has raised a critical question: whether the country’s preparedness measures can protect communities far from major hospitals, laboratories and transport hubs.

The suspected case in Wajir tested negative, according to county officials, easing fears of wider transmission. Yet the incident highlighted the importance of local health facilities being able to recognise suspected infections, isolate patients safely and communicate reliable information to residents.

For communities near Kenya’s borders, preparedness requires more than screening travellers at airports and official crossings.

It also depends on trained health workers, appropriate protective equipment, functioning isolation facilities and clear referral procedures. Residents must know where to seek care and how to respond when health authorities raise the alarm.

Garad Saney Mohamed, communications director for Wajir county, told Al Jazeera that the county had established an isolation centre in Wajir town and formed a rapid response team to strengthen its preparedness.

He said the county was also using radio campaigns, community health promoters, school health programmes and posters to raise awareness about Ebola. A preparedness plan and budget had been put in place, he added.

However, the county did not provide details on the isolation centre’s capacity, the number of health workers trained specifically in Ebola response or the budget allocated to these efforts. Without that information, it is difficult to assess whether the county has the personnel and resources needed to manage suspected infections safely or respond to a wider outbreak.

The suspected case involved a 20-year-old man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo through Uganda before reaching his home in Wajir on September 20. He was assessed at Habaswein Subcounty Hospital in Wajir South after presenting with a severe febrile illness.

His sample tested negative for Ebola, according to county officials. He was to remain under observation while receiving medical care.

The case prompted precautionary action, but it does not establish whether Wajir’s wider preparedness systems would be sufficient during an outbreak. That would depend on factors including the availability of protective equipment, staff trained in infection prevention and control, safe sample transport and reliable links between local facilities and designated testing laboratories.

Wajir’s proximity to Somalia, which lies 110km (70 miles) to the east, and the movement of people and goods across the border make surveillance and public communication particularly important. Screening at formal entry points remains essential, but it cannot replace the ability of local health facilities and community health workers to recognise warning signs and guide people towards appropriate care.

Kenya’s national response intensified after an Ebola case was linked to a Kenyan travelling from the Democratic Republic of the Congo through Uganda. The patient arrived in Nairobi on October 3, was diagnosed with Bundibugyo virus of the disease and died on October 5, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Kenya notified the WHO on October 6.

The patient had fallen ill while living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and travelled by road to Kampala before flying to Nairobi. Laboratory tests at the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute confirmed the infection, according to the Ministry of Health.

On October 14, Kenya confirmed a second case of Bundibugyo virus disease involving a 39-year-old man who was a close family member of the first patient. He was already in quarantine and under daily monitoring when he developed symptoms, including fever, fatigue and joint pains, on October 13.

Laboratory tests confirmed the infection, and he was transferred to a designated treatment centre for supportive care. The Ministry of Health said the two cases were linked and there was no evidence of transmission in the wider community.

Authorities subsequently intensified surveillance at points of entry, contact tracing and public communication. The negative test result in Wajir underscored the importance of investigating suspected infections promptly and using laboratory testing to establish whether the virus is present.

As of October 6, Kenya had screened 652,584 travellers, tested 267 samples and trained 4,971 healthcare workers in Ebola prevention and management, according to the Ministry of Health.

By October 12, the WHO reported that more than 665,000 travellers had been screened and 127 contacts had been listed, with 94 in quarantine. Five laboratories had been designated to test for the disease, and nearly 5,000 health workers had received training.

These figures demonstrate the scale of the national response. But the number of travellers screened or health workers trained does not, on its own, establish how effectively those resources are distributed or whether individual counties can manage suspected infections.

For Wajir, the key questions concern the readiness of local facilities, the availability of trained personnel and protective equipment, and the speed with which samples can be transported for testing. The county has outlined the measures it has taken, but the available information does not provide a complete picture of its operational capacity.

Preparedness means more than the numbers

Health workers need to recognise suspected cases, follow infection-prevention protocols, collect and transport samples safely, and refer patients without exposing others. Facilities must also have appropriate protective equipment and clear procedures for managing suspected infections.

The WHO reported that Kenya’s national preparedness score rose from 66 percent in May to 82 percent in July. The assessment covered measures including surveillance, laboratory testing, isolation and treatment facilities, and trained response teams.

The improvement suggests that preparedness measures had advanced before the imported case was confirmed. However, a national score cannot establish whether every county has the equipment, staffing and referral arrangements needed to respond effectively. Assessments of local capacity are essential to identifying gaps that national figures may not reveal.

The Kenya Red Cross has also supported preparedness and public awareness efforts. Dr Paul Olale, a representative of the organisation, told Al Jazeera about a preparedness assessment. However, the basis of the separate figure attributed to the organisation was not established in the information available for this report, making it difficult to determine what it measured or whether it identified county-level weaknesses.

The organisation has highlighted the need to counter misinformation. During an outbreak, rumours can leave people uncertain about symptoms, how the virus spreads and whether they should seek medical attention.

For residents, information needs to be practical. People should know where to seek care, how to report a suspected illness and what to do while awaiting medical advice. Communication must also address stigma and reassure people that reporting a suspected illness can help protect their families and communities.

Community health promoters, local radio stations, schools and trusted community leaders can help deliver information in languages and formats residents understand. But awareness campaigns are most effective when they are consistent and backed by health services capable of responding promptly to concerns.

Wajir’s experience illustrates why Kenya’s Ebola preparedness must be measured not only by national screening figures and training totals, but also by the ability of individual counties to respond safely when a suspected case emerges.

An isolation centre, a rapid response team and public awareness campaigns are important components of an effective response. Their existence alone, however, does not establish whether facilities have adequate equipment, staff can follow established protocols or residents can access reliable information when they need it.

Kenya has demonstrated its ability to mobilise a national response, expand screening and undertake laboratory testing. The challenge is ensuring that these measures translate into effective protection beyond major transport hubs, including in remote communities where access to healthcare and timely information may be more difficult.

Dr Mary Muthoni, Kenya’s principal secretary for public health and professional standards, underscored the importance of protecting frontline staff in remarks delivered on behalf of Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, according to a WHO statement released on October 12.

“No health worker in this country should be asked to attend to a suspected Ebola case without the right protective equipment.”

Wajir’s health facilities are on the front line of detecting and responding to suspected infectious disease cases [File: Hafsa Sheikh/Al Jazeera]
Questions remain over how prepared remote communities such as Wajir county are to respond to a potential Ebola outbreak [File: Hafsa Sheikh/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Can drinking coriander water help in melting belly fat?
articles.summary: Whether you are trying to fix your health or simply want to lose weight, just starting with one fad drink in the morning may not work like a miracle!
articles.body: Whether you are trying to fix your health or simply want to lose weight, just starting with one fad drink in the morning may not work like a miracle! And that’s the same thing with coriander water, which has many benefits for health but cannot totally melt away the stubborn belly fat. In fact, it is one of the biggest myths that one morning drink can fix and melt visceral body fat in just one or two days. However, being consistent with diet and workouts and then adding coriander water (dhaniya water) may effectively help in reducing waistline. Coriander water has gained massive popularity as a miracle belly fat burner; this is because of the compounds in coriander. Here’s all you need to know about it…What study saysNo beverage or food can target or melt fat from a specific area of the body, such as the belly. According to research published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, localized fat reduction is a biological impossibility. When the body enters a caloric deficit, it mobilizes stored triglycerides from fat cells across the entire body, governed by genetics, hormones, and overall energy balance, not by localized digestive activity.What coriander water actually does for the digestive systemCoriander seeds (Coriandrum sativum) contain bioactive compounds, including linalool and borneol, which act as natural carminatives. A study published in Digestive Diseases and Sciences noted that coriander extract helps relax tract muscles, aiding in gas relief and improving overall bowel motility. By easing indigestion and trapped gas coriander water can visibly flatten a distended stomach giving the appearance of a waistline without actual loss of fat mass.Fluid retention and the diuretic effectMany individuals report initial weight changes after drinking coriander water daily, but this is primarily water weight rather than fat mass. As per another research evaluating extracts in Phytotherapy Research coriander acts as a mild natural diuretic, encouraging the kidneys to excrete excess sodium and fluid. Flushing out excess fluid reduces puffiness and abdominal fluid retention, leading to drops on the bathroom scale.Impact on blood sugar and metabolismControlling glucose spikes plays a role in long-term body composition management. In animal models published in the British Journal of Nutrition, coriander seed supplementation was shown to stimulate insulin secretion and enhance glucose uptake into cells stabilizing blood sugar levels. While stable glucose levels help regulate appetite and reduce energy crashes, human clinical trials have not demonstrated that coriander intake alone significantly boosts resting metabolic rate or drives oxidation.The bottom lineCoriander water is a low-calorie, hydrating beverage that can support healthy digestion, reduce bloating, and help with maintaining fluid balance. However, the current scientific literature confirms that it does not possess burning properties capable of melting belly fat. Sustained reduction of fat requires a consistent energy deficit achieved through balanced nutrition, movement, and lifestyle habits.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Jalna juvenile gets six-month community service for kidnapping 13-year-old, demanding Rs 5 cr ransom
articles.summary: Jalna Juvenile Justice Board orders six months’ community service for juvenile convicted of kidnapping a 13-year-old and demanding Rs 5 crore ransom; boy rescued safe.
articles.body: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: A juvenile found guilty of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy and demanding a ransom of Rs 5 crore has been directed by Juvenile Justice Board, Jalna, to perform community service at the children’s ward of the district general hospital for six months.In an order passed on Monday, the board directed the juvenile to render community service every Monday and Wednesday. The juvenile was held guilty under IPC sections related to kidnapping, kidnapping for ransom, voluntarily causing hurt, criminal intimidation, common intention and criminal conspiracy.The order followed a trial in which the prosecution examined 17 witnesses, including the complainant, the victim, panch witnesses, then additional superintendent of police Ayush Nopani and investigating officer B B Narode. Assistant public prosecutor Atik E Parkote represented the prosecution.According to the prosecution, the incident occurred on June 25, 2024, when the child left home for school at 8am in the morning but never reached class. The father had left for his shop after the boy left for school. Later that day, at 11.45am, the father received a call from unidentified persons claiming to have the boy in their custody and demanding Rs 5 crore for his release. The callers allegedly threatened to kill the child if the ransom was not paid.After being alerted, then additional superintendent of police Ayush Nopani formed two teams to trace the child and apprehend the accused. Police laid a trap and arrested two accused when they arrived to collect the ransom money. The boy was rescued safely from a van and reunited with his family.The prosecution alleged that the child was confined for several hours at an undisclosed location. During the ordeal, he was allegedly slapped and punched, his mouth restrained with a handkerchief, and he was threatened with death if the ransom demand was not met.Following the investigation, sub-inspector B B Narode filed the final report before Juvenile Justice Board. The board, headed by principal magistrate S N Pund and members A M Dhannawat and R B Jagtap, considered the evidence and arguments before delivering the order.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. articles.title: Gangster Dilawar’s aide on ventilator after health deteriorates in Harsul jail
articles.summary: Syed Nazer Ali, aide of jailed gangster Shaikh Imran “Dilawar” Mehandi, fell ill in Harsul Central Prison and was shifted to GMCH Aurangabad, now on ventilator.
articles.body: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: Syed Nazer Ali, a close associate of jailed gangster Shaikh Imran Mehandi, alias Dilawar, and a co-accused in several high-profile murder cases, is battling for life after his health suddenly deteriorated inside Harsul Central Prison. He was shifted to Govt Medical College and Hospital on Sunday evening and remains on ventilator support.Doctors said following preliminary examinations, Nazer Ali underwent dialysis before being placed on a ventilator. “He continues to remain under medical supervision,” a senior GMCH doctor said.Confirming the development, Harsul Central Prison in-charge superintendent Anil Khamkar said, “Nazer Ali, a life convict lodged in barrack 8 of the old circle, complained of dizziness and started vomiting. He was shifted to GMCH immediately and is now on ventilator support.”Nazer Ali is considered one of the key members of Dilawar’s gang and is a co-accused in multiple murder cases registered in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in 2012. The cases include the murders of former corporator Salim Qureshi, Nilesh Mhatre, Shaikh Naser, Sindubai Mhatre and Sirajuddin.The development comes days after Supreme Court granted relief to Dilawar in the 2012 Salim Qureshi murder case by suspending his life sentence pending disposal of his appeal. The apex court took into account his prolonged incarceration, including 12 years without remission and 18 years with remission.Despite the relief, Dilawar remains behind bars as he stands convicted in another murder case and continues to face trial in three others. Nazer Ali and several other associates are also accused in those cases.The circumstances behind Nazer Ali’s sudden medical emergency were not immediately known.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news.
